opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think sparse autoencoders are a really interesting tool, but I've become more skeptical about treating them as *the* way to represent what's going on inside a model.

The first issue is that an SAE is a model of the model. You train a second network to reconstruct the activations under a sparsity constraint, and the features you get are partly a product of that training setup: the dictionary size, the sparsity penalty, the data you trained on. Change those and features split, merge, or vanish. People call this "feature splitting." So it's not obvious that what you're finding is the model's true set of concepts rather than an artifact of how you chose to decompose it.

Second, reconstruction is imperfect. There's usually a meaningful chunk of variance the SAE doesn't capture, sometimes called "dark matter." When you splice the reconstruction back in, downstream performance drops noticeably. If the part you can't explain is the part doing the interesting computation, that's a real problem for claiming you understand the model.

Third, and this is what I care about most, there's a gap between features that look interpretable and features that are useful. You can label a feature "this fires on French text" and it looks great in a dashboard. But when you try to use SAE features for practical things like steering behavior or detecting a concept, they often don't beat much simpler baselines: linear probes, difference-in-means directions, or just prompting the model. If the goal of interpretability is to do something with your understanding, like controlling or debugging models, then we should be benchmarking against those baselines, and SAEs haven't consistently won.

Fourth, the labels are often generated automatically, by having another LLM look at top-activating examples. That tends to overstate how clean a feature is, because the top activations are the most prototypical cases. The weaker activations can be much messier.

And finally, SAEs mostly give you a static snapshot of representations at one layer. They don't directly tell you about the computation: how information flows, which components causally produce a behavior. For that you need causal methods like interventions, patching, and circuit analysis. Transcoders and cross-layer variants are trying to address this, which is promising.

So I don't think SAEs are useless. They're good for exploration and for generating hypotheses. But I'd treat them as one tool among many, and I'd want interpretability claims to be backed by causal tests and comparisons to simple baselines, not just by features that look nice.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that sparse autoencoders were a really exciting idea, and they still have their uses, but a lot of us in the interpretability community have gotten more skeptical over the past year or two about whether they're actually giving us the "true" units of computation inside a model.

The basic premise is that you take the activations at some layer, and you train this dictionary where each entry is supposed to be a monosemantic feature, something like "the Golden Gate Bridge" or "code in Python." And you do get a lot of features that look really clean when you read them. But there are a few problems.

One is that the features you get depend heavily on the hyperparameters. If you change the dictionary size, you get a different decomposition. A feature that was one thing at eight thousand latents gets split into five things at sixty-four thousand, and it's not obvious which level of granularity is the one the model actually uses. There isn't a privileged basis the SAE is recovering. It's imposing one.

The second issue is reconstruction error. Even good SAEs leave behind a chunk of the variance, and when you actually run the model with the reconstructed activations swapped in, you often get a noticeable hit to performance. So there's some part of what the model is doing that lives in that residual, and we're just not accounting for it. That's a sign that the sparse linear superposition assumption is at best approximate.

The third thing, which I care about a lot, is that SAEs are unsupervised. They find directions that are good for reconstruction, not directions that are causally relevant for a behavior you care about. So you can get a feature that lights up on a concept but doesn't actually do anything when you intervene on it, or the thing that controls the behavior is spread across many features in a way that's hard to read off. When people have done head-to-head comparisons, say, on steering or on finding the representation of some concept, SAE features often don't beat much simpler baselines like linear probes or even just prompting.

And then there's the more basic conceptual worry that maybe the model's internal variables aren't sparse and linear in the way we'd like. Some things probably are, and that's why SAEs find them. But features might be encoded in nonlinear ways, or they might be defined relationally, in terms of what other features are active, and a static dictionary over one layer can't capture that.

So my view is that SAEs are a decent exploratory tool for getting a feel for what's represented, but I wouldn't treat the features as ground truth. If you have a specific hypothesis about what the model is computing, you're often better off with more targeted, causally grounded methods that let you actually test that hypothesis rather than hoping the right feature falls out of an unsupervised decomposition.

astra-6.text:
I think the main limitation is that a sparse autoencoder gives you a particular decomposition of a model’s activations, and it’s easy to mistake that decomposition for the actual structure of the model’s computation.

You train it to reconstruct activations using a small number of features at a time. But you’re choosing the number of features and how strongly to enforce sparsity. Those choices affect what you find: one feature might split into several more specific features as you increase the size of the autoencoder. So there isn’t necessarily a unique, canonical list of concepts that you’ve recovered.

There’s also a tradeoff between sparsity and reconstruction. If you make the representation very sparse, you can lose information that matters to the model’s behavior. And even if a feature has a nice, human-readable interpretation, that doesn’t establish what causal role it plays. A feature activating on examples involving deception, say, doesn’t by itself mean you’ve found the mechanism responsible for deceptive behavior.

So I’d treat sparse autoencoders as tools for generating hypotheses. They can give you useful things to investigate, but you still need interventions and an account of how those features interact across layers to explain what the model is actually doing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key limitation is that a sparse autoencoder gives you a particular decomposition of the model’s activations, and it’s tempting to treat that decomposition as the model’s actual internal vocabulary. That’s a stronger claim than we can usually justify.

You’re choosing how many features to learn and how sparse you want them to be. Change those choices, and a concept might split into several features or get bundled together with something else. So even if a feature has a nice, interpretable label, that doesn’t mean you’ve discovered a unique, fundamental unit of computation.

There’s also a gap between reconstructing activations and explaining behavior. An autoencoder can reconstruct an activation reasonably well while missing a small component that matters a lot for a particular prediction. And identifying a feature that correlates with some concept doesn’t tell you how the model uses it. For that, you need interventions and an understanding of how features interact across layers.

So I see sparse autoencoders as a useful tool for generating hypotheses about what’s happening inside a model. But the readable features are the beginning of an explanation, rather than the explanation itself.
